los.text: Recognise common anatomical variants arising during the development of the urogenital system
los.html:
• Background: the kidney forms in the pelvis from the ureteric bud (off the mesonephric duct) meeting the metanephric blastema, then ascends to T12–L3, rotating medially and picking up new arteries as it goes.
VariantCauseWhy it matters
Duplex kidney / double ureterUreteric bud splits (bifid) or two buds ariseUpper-pole ureter opens lower and more medially (may obstruct or form a ureterocele); lower-pole ureter refluxes
Horseshoe kidneyLower poles fuse; ascent stopped by the IMAStones, infection, PUJ obstruction
Pelvic kidneyFailed ascentMistaken for a pelvic mass; trauma risk
Renal agenesisNo ureteric budBilateral → oligohydramnios, Potter sequence (lung hypoplasia)
Accessory renal arteriesPersisting vessels from ascentEnd arteries; can cross and obstruct the ureter
Ectopic ureterOpens into vagina/urethraConstant dribbling in girls
Urachal remnantsAllantois/urachus fails to closeUrine from the umbilicus, cyst or sinus
HypospadiasUrethral folds fail to fuseMeatus on the underside of the penis
Posterior urethral valvesMucosal folds in the male urethraBladder outlet obstruction in boys

los.text: Recall the relationships of the kidneys and ureters to other abdominal and pelvic structures and discuss the significance of these relationships with respect to urinary stones
los.html:
KidneysRetroperitoneal, T12–L3; right lower than left (liver).
Posterior relations
  • Diaphragm (and above it the pleura and 12th rib: risk in biopsy or nephrectomy), psoas major, quadratus lumborum, transversus abdominis
  • Subcostal, iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves.
Ureter course
  • on psoas, crossed in front by the gonadal vessels
  • → crosses the pelvic brim at the common iliac bifurcation (over the sacroiliac joint)
  • → down the pelvic side wall
  • → turns in at the ischial spine
  • → passes under the uterine artery ("water under the bridge") or under the vas deferens
  • → enters the bladder obliquely.
NarrowingWhere stones lodge
Pelviureteric junctionTop of the ureter
Pelvic brimCrossing the iliac vessels
Vesicoureteric junctionNarrowest point
PainLoin to groin (T11–L2); genitofemoral nerve refers it to the scrotum or labia.
Imaging
  • on X-ray the ureter runs over the tips of the lumbar transverse processes, the sacroiliac joint and the ischial spine
  • Non-contrast CT KUB is the standard test.
Surgical riskUreter injured when ligating the uterine artery at hysterectomy.

los.text: Discuss micturition with regard to the consequences of obstruction of the ureter (kidney stones), and the urethra (common in elderly males due to enlargement of the prostate gland)
los.html:
Ureteric obstruction (stone)
  • Upstream dilatation (hydroureter, hydronephrosis)
  • Colicky pain from peristalsis against the block
  • Infection (an obstructed infected kidney is an emergency: nephrostomy or stent)
  • Loss of function if prolonged
  • Both sides → post-renal AKI.
Urethral obstruction (BPH)The prostate's transition zone grows around the prostatic urethra → bladder outlet obstruction.
EffectDetail
Voiding symptomsHesitancy, poor stream, straining, dribbling, incomplete emptying
Storage symptomsFrequency, urgency, nocturia
Bladder changesDetrusor thickening (trabeculation), diverticula
Residual urineUTIs, bladder stones
Acute retentionPainful, can't pass urine: catheterise
Chronic retentionPainless, overflow incontinence; high pressure → bilateral hydronephrosis, renal failure

los.text: Describe the course of the ureter with respect to other structures, and describe the pathway of urine from the renal pyramids to the urinary bladder
los.html:
1. Renal papillaCollecting ducts open at the tip of each pyramid.
2. Minor calyx(7–14)Major calyx (2–3) → renal pelvis.
3. Ureter(~25 cm)Urine moved by peristalsis.
4. Vesicoureteric junctionThe ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall, acting as a flap valve against reflux.
5. Bladder(trigone)Urethra.
Course
  • Abdominal part on psoas behind the gonadal vessels (right: behind duodenum and right colic vessels; left: behind the sigmoid mesocolon)
  • Pelvic part on the side wall in front of the internal iliac artery, under the vas or uterine artery.
Blood supplySegmental from renal, gonadal, aortic, iliac and vesical/uterine arteries, linked along its length; stripping the adventitia risks ischaemia.

los.text: Recognise the bladder and its parts (including the ureteric openings), and identify the overlying peritoneum and the anatomical relationships of the bladder in male and female pelvises
los.html:
PartsApex (in front; median umbilical ligament = urachus), body, fundus/base (behind), neck (into the urethra).
Trigone
  • Smooth triangle on the inside of the base between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice
  • Does not stretch.
  • The rest of the lining is folded (rugae).
WallDetrusor (interlacing smooth muscle).
Peritoneum
  • Covers only the superior surface
  • a filling bladder rises above the pubis and peels peritoneum off the anterior wall, so a suprapubic catheter can go in without entering the peritoneal cavity.
RelationMaleFemale
FrontPubic symphysis, retropubic spaceSame
BehindSeminal vesicles, vas ampullae, rectum (rectovesical pouch)Uterus (vesicouterine pouch), cervix, vagina
BelowProstatePelvic floor, urethra
AbovePeritoneum, small bowel, sigmoidBody of the uterus resting on it
Capacity~400–600 mL; first urge at ~150–300 mL.
RuptureExtraperitoneal with pelvic fractures; intraperitoneal (dome) from a blow to a full bladder.

los.text: Name the nerve fibres that innervate the bladder and its sphincters, recall their paths, and describe the mechanism of micturition
los.html:
FibresOriginEffect
ParasympatheticPelvic splanchnic nerves, S2–4Detrusor contracts (M3), internal sphincter relaxes: voiding
SympatheticT11–L2 via hypogastric nervesDetrusor relaxes (β3), bladder neck contracts (α1): storage; stops retrograde ejaculation
SomaticPudendal nerve, S2–4External urethral sphincter contracts (voluntary)
AfferentStretch receptors → pelvic nerves → S2–4Fullness signals up to the pontine micturition centre
1. FillingSympathetic and pudendal tone keep the outlet shut; the detrusor stays relaxed.
2. DecisionThe frontal cortex decides it's a good time and releases the pontine micturition centre.
3. VoidingParasympathetic detrusor contraction while sympathetic and pudendal output switch off; sphincters relax.
LesionBladder result
Above the pons (stroke, frontal)Urge incontinence (uninhibited bladder)
Spinal cord above S2Reflex bladder, detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia
Sacral cord / cauda equinaAtonic bladder: painless retention with overflow

los.text: Recognise the anatomical parts of the urethra in males and females and link those parts to continence and catheterisation
los.html:
• Female urethra: ~4 cm, straight, through the pelvic floor to the meatus in the vestibule, in front of the vaginal opening.
    • Short → more UTIs
    • easy to catheterise.
Male partLength / features
PreprostaticBladder neck; internal sphincter (smooth, sympathetic)
ProstaticWidest, most distensible; ejaculatory and prostatic ducts open on the seminal colliculus
MembranousShortest and narrowest; surrounded by the external urethral sphincter (deep perineal pouch)
SpongyLongest; in the corpus spongiosum; bulbourethral glands open into it; ends at the navicular fossa and meatus
Continence
  • External sphincter (voluntary) and bladder neck in men
  • in women the external sphincter plus urethral support from the pelvic floor (weakened by childbirth → stress incontinence).
Male catheterisation
  • Hold the penis upwards to straighten the curve
  • Lubricant with anaesthetic
  • Expect resistance at the external sphincter and an enlarged prostate
  • Inflate the balloon only once urine flows (not in the prostatic urethra).
